title: Post Scarcity
summary: If abundance uncouples survival from labour, what happens to the city built around work? A park and a vertical neighbourhood at Center Square.
body: A thesis about what a city becomes when scarcity stops organising it. It takes the premise seriously — a fifteen-hour week, universal basic income, goods at near-zero marginal cost — and follows it down to a single block of Philadelphia.

The answer is a park at Center Square, west of City Hall, and a building lifted above it: a structural frame treated as a street grid, filled with programs that self-organise by proximity rather than by zoning class.
Awarded the 2025 Pearson Prize Silver Medal for best Drexel architectural thesis.

chapters.title: Can Architects Shape the Future?
chapters.standfirst: Or are architectural movements only ever a response?
body: A thesis in architecture is a design project or research proposal that explores a central idea. Mine starts with a question I could not answer: whether architects lead change, or arrive after it.
To ask it properly I had to invent a future to design for.

chapters.title: Defining Post Scarcity
body: The economy shifts through decentralised production, universal basic income, zero-marginal-cost goods and a sharing culture. Work settles near fifteen hours a week, concentrated in creative and critical-thinking fields.
Value moves toward social capital, environmental stewardship and community well-being. And scarcity relocates: what becomes scarce is time, privacy, natural features and genuine experience.

chapters.title: A Week Reclaimed
chapters.standfirst: Six hours a day move out of work and into everything else.
body: Set the reality week against the post-scarcity week and the arithmetic is stark — 1,717.5 hours a year returned. Rebuilt as program, the city's demands move with it.

chapters.title: Better Pastimes
chapters.standfirst: More free time does not guarantee a better life.
body: The average American spends 2 hours 18 minutes on social media, 1 hour 19 on games and 2 hours watching television — inside a day with less than six hours of personal time.
That retreat into screens reads as a failure of the public realm. So: what can architects do to encourage better pastimes?

chapters.title: Counterpoint
chapters.standfirst: Two independent lines, played at once.
body: Counterpoint uses contrast to create interest, choice and harmony. It does not imply opposition.
Four run through the project: grid against greenspace, greenspace against built space, built space against program, and program against program.

quote.text: Counterpoint doesn't imply opposition — it highlights contrast to create interest, choice, and harmony between two or more independent ideas.

chapters.title: Precedents
chapters.standfirst: Where the grid is broken, the city is at its best.
body: Philadelphia's grid is rarely interrupted, and where it is, the results are among its most memorable places — a preserved Lenape trail cutting through South Philadelphia, a square whose walks ignore the street lines, a pocket park mid-block.
For built space against program, two buildings: Toyo Ito's Sendai Mediatheque, and Kunsthaus Graz.

blocks.title: Rittenhouse Square, East Passyunk, John F. Collins Park, Sendai Mediatheque, Kunsthaus Graz

chapters.title: Proximity Zoning
chapters.standfirst: Zoning by how well things sit together, not by what they are.
body: American zoning is incompatible with a post-scarcity society. At its best it prevents harmful adjacencies; at its worst it has been used to exclude and segregate.

Proximity zoning is the alternative: a tool that reads the attributes of each program and scores how well it fits its surroundings. Not a black box, and not a replacement for the designer — decision support, and the score can be appealed.

chapters.title: Philadelphia
body: That Philadelphia's greenspace was in poor condition. Measured against Vienna and Copenhagen, its parks and plazas were lacking considerably more than expected.

chapters.title: Center Square
chapters.standfirst: A park at the heart of the city, west of City Hall.
body: The site carries 113,000 transit riders past it every day — 30,000 on the Market–Frankford line, 57,000 on Broad Street, 26,000 through Suburban Station. No other ground in the city is handed that many people before it opens.
The park breaks the grid deliberately: soft lines against the rectilinear order, an amphitheatre, a plaza at LOVE, a rec centre and a playscape.

chapters.title: The Frame
chapters.standfirst: The structural grid treated as a street grid.
body: Uniform cubes. At its full 36-foot height the bay suits outdoor space, industry or sport; halved to 18 feet it takes schools and workshops; in thirds at 12 feet, apartments and small retail.
The building is lifted so only the cores touch down, and the park runs beneath it. The elevator becomes the lobby.

chapters.title: Clusters
body: Placed by proximity zoning, programs form clusters around a shared centre — a vertical fifteen-minute neighbourhood where daily needs are close but the pull outward stays intact.

chapters.title: Through the Building
chapters.standfirst: A day spent moving through it.
body: The market and its roof-top piazza, the studios and family units, the school and community centre, the co-working tower with fifteen storeys of green wall filtering the hydroponic farms below.
Moving between them should feel like walking a street, not passing exits on a highway.

chapters.title: Can Architects Shape the Future?
body: This was never about designing a fully realistic building. It continues a conversation begun long before me.

Abundance alone does not guarantee quality of life. It is thoughtfully designed, interconnected places that let us feel the benefit of it — and that draw us out into the world rather than back to a screen.

quote.text: The future cannot be predicted, but futures can be invented.
